tagline: Black mountains above a blue Adriatic
overview:
Montenegro is one of Europe's smallest countries, a piece of the Balkan coast about the size of Connecticut, wedged between Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Kosovo, and Albania. Its name means black mountain, and the land earns it: dark pine ridges and bare gray limestone rise within a few kilometers of the Adriatic Sea.

About 620,000 people live here, most speaking Montenegrin, a language closely related to Serbian, Croatian, and Bosnian. Podgorica is the capital and largest city, while the old royal town of Cetinje, high in the hills, remains the ceremonial capital. Montenegro is a parliamentary republic, independent since a referendum in 2006.

In summer the walled seaside towns of Kotor and Budva fill with visitors who swim in water clear enough to see the seabed and take boats out to tiny island churches. Inland, shepherds still drive sheep up to mountain pastures when the snow melts, and villages cure ham and make cheese much as they always have.
landAndNature: The Bay of Kotor cuts deep inland between cliffs, a drowned river canyon so steep that visitors often mistake it for a fjord. Behind it the Dinaric Alps climb past 2,500 meters at Bobotov Kuk in Durmitor National Park, where glacial lakes sit ringed by pine forest and the Tara River has carved a canyon roughly 1,300 meters deep. Much of the rock is karst, limestone riddled with caves, sinkholes, and underground rivers. Lake Skadar, the largest lake in the Balkans, is a maze of water lilies and reeds where pelicans nest. Bears, wolves, lynx, and chamois live in the forests, and while the coast keeps dry Mediterranean summers, the mountains get deep snow.
peopleAndCulture: Montenegrins have a Balkan reputation for tall stature, pride, and unhurried hospitality; the local word inat, meaning stubbornness, is worn almost as a badge. Most people belong to Orthodox Christian churches, alongside Muslim and Catholic communities. Food changes with altitude: grilled meats, smoked ham called pršut, and sheep cheese in the highlands; fish, squid, and olive oil on the coast. Singers called guslars still perform epic poems to the scrape of the gusle, a one-stringed fiddle. Water polo is the national passion, and Montenegro's team wins European medals despite the country's tiny population, with basketball and soccer close behind. Summer brings brass bands, carnival parades, and a flower festival in Kotor.
history: Illyrian tribes lived here before Rome took the coast. In the Middle Ages the Slavic realm of Duklja, later called Zeta, grew up in these mountains, and after the Ottoman Empire swept across the Balkans, Montenegro's prince-bishops held out in the highlands around Cetinje for centuries. Its independence was recognized in 1878. In 1918 Montenegro joined the new kingdom that became Yugoslavia, and after World War II it was one of Yugoslavia's six republics under the communist leader Tito. When Yugoslavia broke apart in the 1990s, wars across the region killed tens of thousands of people; Montenegro remained joined to Serbia and was affected by the fighting and by international sanctions. It voted narrowly for independence in 2006 and joined NATO in 2017.
funFacts: Montenegro's name in Montenegrin, Crna Gora, translates literally as black mountain, a description of its dark forested slopes.
The Tara River canyon is the deepest in Europe, dropping about 1,300 meters below the plateau around it.
Our Lady of the Rocks, an island in the Bay of Kotor, was built up over centuries by sailors dropping stones into the sea.
Montenegro's water polo team, drawn from about 620,000 people, regularly beats countries fifty times larger.
Sveti Stefan, a stone fishing village on a rocky islet, is joined to the mainland only by a narrow sandbar.
